newsitem.title: ITALY: U.S, Italy agree on NATO; at odds over Iran, Libya.
newsitem.headline: U.S, Italy agree on NATO; at odds over Iran, Libya.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Italian leaders made no progress on Sunday on rows over Iran, Libya and Cuba but were in broad agreement on NATO expansion plans, Turkey and keeping the alliance southern military command in American hands, U.S. officials said.

The two governments also agreed on opposition to a NATO mini-summit proposed by France and that a NATO summit to decide new members in July should go forward regardless of whether the alliance completes a charter with Russia defining a new special relationshop, officials said.
Albright, the first female U.S. secretary of state, made Rome the first stop on her first overseas trip, taking her to nine major world capitals over 11 days.
At a news conference with Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, she said "we came to agreement on a whole set of issues especially NATO enlargement and the NATO-Russian charter."
Dini said the two ministers agreed an enlarged NATO was not intended as a threat to Russia and should not be viewed as such.

A major focus of the alliance is trying to assure Russia, where official opposition to NATO taking in new members is fierce, that expansion will enhance the security of all of Europe and not be directed against Moscow.

Albright acknowledged that in meetings that also included Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Defence Minister Benjiamino Andreatta "we covered some issues on which we did not have total agreement," including Iran, Iraq, Libya and Cuba.
"I feel from our perspective very strongly that supporting states that support state terrorism is a genuine problem for us," Albright said.

Washington considers Iran and Libya state sponsors of terrorism. It also believes Iran is seeking to acquire nuclear capability while Iraq continues to try to rebuild its military arsenal in contravention of U.N. sanctions after the Gulf War.
The United States has accused Libya of harbouring two suspects blamed for the 1988 bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland.
U.S. law permits sanctions against companies doing business in Iran and Libya.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said later that especially in the meeting with Dini, "there was a very long conversation about the (European) critical dialogue with Iran, about Italian relations with Libya and a little less disagreement on Iraq."

Albright told the Italians "we don't see that the critical dialogue is working...We see Iran embarking on military modernisation, attempting to acquire weapons of mass destruction and (engaging in) direct and incontrovertible support for terrorism in the Middle East," Burns said.
She "really leaned on each of them. She was very direct," but there was no change in the position of Italy, which imports 42 percent of its oil from Iran and Libya, he said.

Italian leaders, especially Dini, took issue with controversial U.S. anti-Cuba legislation and explained the role Italian telecommunications firm Stet is playing on Cuba, the communist island 90 miles from American shores.

The U.S. law allows Washington to bar executives and shareholders of foreign companies from entering the United States. It affects companies that are using properties confiscated during the communist revolution in 1959 from Cubans who are now U.S. citizens.
The law also allows U.S. citizens to sue foreign companies that use those confiscated properties but that provision has been suspended for the moment.
Stet has been warned it could be punished under U.S. law and U.S. officials said they expect Washington to act officially at some point.

U.S. officials said Italian leaders, especially prime minister Prodi, expressed concern about Turkey, whose leadership is putting a more Islamic stamp on the secular country, and Cyprus, where Turkey-Greece tensions have been raising alarms.

The two governments agree it is critical that efforts must be made by the European Union to tie Turkey closely to the west and that an intensive new effort must be made to resolve the division between Greeks and Turks on Cyprus, officials said.
Albright later flies to Bonn for talks with German leaders and then travels to Paris, Brussels, London, Moscow, Seoul, Tokyo and Beijing.
